catalog_quote: Tone is contrastive in Tira, and can be used to distinguish between different lexemes, or different forms of the same lexeme. This is illustrated by the minimal pairs listed in (16)–(17), two word pairs which differ tonally. ... We have seen no evidence of lexical tone on verbs so far, so the present discussion will be focused on lexical tone on nouns, and is based on our current database of about 200 noun lexemes. [p. 80] ... While Stevenson (1942/2009) had discovered some tonal minimal pairs in Tira, including the ones in (11), he did not go into much detail about the tone system. One page is dedicated to a discussion about possible tone or stress and its relationship to intonation, where he observes that “inherent tone plays little part in distinguishing words” (Stevenson 1942/2009, p. 17). He admits that the details would still need to be worked out, but tentatively concludes that “Tira is not a tone language in the fullest sense of the term” (Stevenson 1942/2009, p. 17). ... In contrast, tone is the main topic tackled by Watters (1993), who shows that “Tira has phonologically significant, contrastive pitch” (Watters 1993, p. 88) and therefore concludes that Tira is in fact a tone language. [p. 72]

new_statements.rule_in_words: No accessible source says where word stress falls. The modern primary descriptions (Kaldhol 2024; Kaldhol, Rose & Simmons 2025) treat Tira as a two-tone language (H, L; word-final H͡L contour; H-spreading across words) and say nothing about word stress. The only stress-related content is second-hand: Stevenson's 1942 grammar (published 2009) has one page (p. 17) on 'possible tone or stress and its relationship to intonation', doubting that Tira is a tone language 'in the fullest sense'; Watters 1993 (abstract only accessible) discusses 'the relationships between tone, length and loudness' in ch. 3. Neither of those pages could be opened.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; no stress rule is given.
new_statements.domain_note: Kaldhol 2024 and Kaldhol et al. 2025 describe the Kadar dialect (Kauda area) from one speaker (Himidan Hassen), elicited words and sentences; Watters 1993 is a single-speaker case study of the El Akdar dialect; Stevenson's material was collected c. 1942. The quoted passage is Kaldhol's summary of Stevenson, not a first-hand stress statement; treat the stress question as unresolved.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog tira1254 (ISO tic) is language-level with no dialect children. Sources differ in variety: Kaldhol 2024 and Kaldhol, Rose & Simmons 2025 describe the Kadar dialect (Kauda area; single speaker Himidan Hassen, born 1991 in Komo); Watters 1993 is a single-speaker study of the El Akdar dialect; Stevenson's grammar (ms. 1942-43, publ. 2009) reflects 1940s speech; Alaki 2017 covers 'Litiro of Tombore'. Not to be confused with Tirax (maee1241, Vanuatu) or Tiro/Tira names elsewhere.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Group-level statement only (ch. 18a treats Koalib-Moro incl. Tira, Talodi-Masakin and Lafofa together): the role of tone is 'not yet fully investigated' but a few lexical tone doublets are recorded; following Stevenson, expiratory ('dynamic') stress combined with high or low tone plays a greater role than syllabic pitch, though not equally in all languages of the group; no placement rule is given and the examples are unmarked for tone and stress; nothing is said about Tira in particular (Tira appears only in noun-class and verb-derivation examples). sources.note: Citation and citing context only: Kaldhol 2024 ch. 3 fn. 13 reports that this ms 'proposes a tentative phonological analysis of the lack of High tone spreading' between imperfective auxiliaries and the verb root 'by treating the auxiliaries as clitics, with their High tones being subject to the OCP when the auxiliaries are bound to the verb root'; i.e. a dedicated study of the cross-word H-tone spreading process (the process the catalog prose already mentions) and its blocking contexts.

tone.summary: H-tone spreading (rightward, across words) and OCP-based blocking; presupposes the 2-level H/L system.
